planting.note: Direct sow onto bare, saturated mud in fall so winter cold breaks dormancy; this winter annual overwinters as a low rosette and flowers the following spring before summer heat sets in.

directions: Pennsylvania bittercress colonizes the cold, constantly saturated mud of spring branches and seep flushes across the Ozark and Ouachita highlands, forming loose rosettes of pinnately divided leaves that send up branching stems of small white four-petaled flowers from early spring into fall. It thrives where groundwater keeps the soil perpetually wet and cool, such as the edge of a spring run, rain garden low point, or shaded streambank, and declines quickly if the root zone is allowed to dry even briefly. Plants self-sow readily onto fresh wet mud and persist as a low, unobtrusive groundcover at the saturated margins of a water feature rather than a showy border plant. It requires no fertilizing and spreads naturally wherever bare, wet mineral soil is exposed.

planting.note: Scatter seed directly onto bare, exposed wet mud after the soil has warmed in spring; this mustard-family annual germinates on freshly disturbed, saturated ground and needs no covering.

directions: Sessile yellowcress is an unassuming native mustard that colonizes muddy gravel bars, drying stream margins, and the edges of Ozark Highlands spring seeps, with smooth, glabrous stems and tiny, nearly petal-less flowers that are easy to overlook among showier seep wildflowers. It is valued less for floral display than for its role as an early pioneer of bare, periodically disturbed wet mud, where it helps stabilize fresh sediment before sedges and other perennials move in. Give it consistently wet, mineral soil with full sun exposure such as a stream-edge mudflat or the drawdown zone of a rain garden, and let it reseed itself on any newly exposed damp ground. It completes its life cycle quickly as the growing season warms and is best used in naturalistic wetland-margin restoration plantings rather than formal beds.

planting.note: Direct sow onto exposed, saturated mud once the soil has warmed; seedlings establish quickly on bare wet ground and need no transplanting.

directions: Yellowseed false pimpernel is a low, branching annual that spreads over the bare, saturated mud of gravel bars and seep margins along Ozark and Ouachita spring-fed streams, bearing small tubular white flowers tinged with lavender and lipped at the mouth. It germinates readily wherever flood or seepage water has freshly exposed mineral soil, making it a useful companion species for the drawdown edge of a constructed bog garden or stream-margin planting. Keep the soil continuously wet to saturated through the growing season, since the plant cannot tolerate a dry spell once established, and allow it to self-sow onto any newly bared wet ground each year. Its diminutive size and quiet coloring make it best suited to naturalistic wetland-edge plantings rather than a conventional flower bed.

planting.note: Direct sow onto bare, saturated mud as soon as seep water begins to recede in spring; this sticky-stemmed annual is one of the first plants to colonize freshly exposed wet ground.

directions: Clammy hedge-hyssop is a small, glandular-sticky annual that pioneers the drying mud margins of Ozark and Ouachita spring pools and seep flushes, carrying whitish, faintly tubular flowers tucked close against the stem among opposite, narrow leaves. Its sticky foliage discourages browsing and helps it persist on the exposed, nutrient-thin mineral soil left behind as seep water levels fluctuate through the season. Plant it in a continuously damp to saturated spot such as the shrinking edge of a spring-fed pool or rain garden basin, where competition from larger wetland plants is naturally limited, and let it self-sow onto freshly bared mud each year. It is a modest but ecologically useful addition to a naturalistic seep or vernal pool planting rather than a conventional ornamental bed.

planting.note: Fall-sow seed onto consistently moist to wet soil for natural winter stratification, or set out divisions in spring; establish along a seep margin, streambank, or rain garden where the soil never fully dries.

directions: Purple-leaf willowherb grows along the wet margins of Ozark and Ouachita spring branches, seep flushes, and streambanks, sending up slender, reddish-tinted stems lined with narrow opposite leaves that often take on a cinnamon-purple cast as the season progresses. Small white to pale pink notched petals open from late summer into fall, later than most seep wildflowers finish blooming, giving pollinators a continued nectar source as the growing season winds down. It spreads gradually by shallow rhizomes in permanently moist to wet, humus-rich soil and is well suited to the saturated fringe of a rain garden, pond, or spring-fed swale rather than ordinary garden beds. Established clumps need no division or fertilizing and tolerate brief flooding without harm.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring onto moist, open ground; this fine-textured annual needs little soil preparation but will not persist where competing vegetation is dense or the ground dries out for long.

directions: Nuttall's mock bishopweed is a finely dissected, lacy-leaved annual of the carrot family that fills wet prairie swales, pond margins, and seep-fed meadow edges across the south-central United States, including the Ozark and Ouachita Interior Highlands. Its thread-like foliage supports flat-topped umbels of tiny white flowers in early to midsummer that closely resemble a miniature Queen Anne's lace, drawing in small native bees and other short-tongued pollinators. It performs best in full sun on consistently moist to wet, open mineral soil, such as the saturated edge of a rain garden or the shallow margin of a seasonally wet meadow, where it self-sows readily on bare damp ground each year. As a larval host plant for black swallowtail butterflies, it adds ecological value alongside its airy, textural presence in a naturalistic wet-meadow planting.
